claim: In eukaryotic cells, stressors reprogram the cellular proteome by activating the integrated stress response (ISR).
source: In eukaryotic cells, stressors reprogram the cellular proteome by activating the integrated stress response (ISR).
evidence: This is a general statement about the ISR that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Stress-sensing kinases phosphorylate eIF2 at serine 51 of the α subunit.
source: The ISR integrates diverse stresses through at least four stress-sensing kinases – PERK, HRI, GCN2, PKR, and perhaps MARK2, via phosphorylation of a single serine, S51 of the α subunit of the translation initiation factor eIF2 (Hinnebusch, 2005; Guo et al., 2020; Dey et al., 2005; Shi et al., 1998; Lu et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Translational control is primarily exerted through a conformational switch in eIF2B from its active A-State to its inhibited I-State upon eIF2-P binding.
source: Previously we showed that translational control is primarily exerted through a conformational switch in eIF2's nucleotide exchange factor, eIF2B, which shifts from its active A-State conformation to its inhibited I-State conformation upon eIF2-P binding, resulting in reduced nucleotide exchange on eIF2 (Schoof et al. 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The eIF2B βH160D mutation mimics the effects of eIF2-P binding by promoting an I-State like conformation.
source: Here, we show functionally and structurally how a single histidine to aspartate point mutation in eIF2B's β subunit (H160D) mimics the effects of eIF2-P binding by promoting an I-State like conformation, resulting in eIF2-P independent activation of the ISR.
evidence: This is the main finding of the manuscript, supported by structural and functional data presented throughout.

claim: The eIF2B βH160D mutation results in eIF2-P independent activation of the ISR.
source: Here, we show functionally and structurally how a single histidine to aspartate point mutation in eIF2B's β subunit (H160D) mimics the effects of eIF2-P binding by promoting an I-State like conformation, resulting in eIF2-P independent activation of the ISR.
evidence: Supported by cellular data showing ISR activation in cells with the mutation.

claim: Phosphorylation of eIF2 leads to a precipitous drop in global protein synthesis.
source: Phosphorylation of eIF2 disrupts this process and leads to a precipitous drop in global protein synthesis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the ISR mechanism.

claim: Translation of stress-responsive mRNAs such as ATF4 is induced during the ISR.
source: Conversely, the translation of a subset of stress-responsive mRNAs, such as ATF4, generally repressed by the presence of 5' UTR upstream open reading frames (uORFs), is induced (Harding et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The ISR has been linked to neurodegenerative diseases.
source: Specifically, the ISR has been linked to neurodegenerative diseases (Ma et al., 2013), brain-injury induced dementia (Chou et al., 2017; Sen et al., 2017), aging (Krukowski et al., 2020), diabetes (Abdulkarim et al., 2015; Harding et al., 2001), and cancer (Nguyen et al., 2018; Koromilas et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The ISR has been linked to brain-injury induced dementia.
source: Specifically, the ISR has been linked to neurodegenerative diseases (Ma et al., 2013), brain-injury induced dementia (Chou et al., 2017; Sen et al., 2017), aging (Krukowski et al., 2020), diabetes (Abdulkarim et al., 2015; Harding et al., 2001), and cancer (Nguyen et al., 2018; Koromilas et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The ISR has been linked to aging.
source: Specifically, the ISR has been linked to neurodegenerative diseases (Ma et al., 2013), brain-injury induced dementia (Chou et al., 2017; Sen et al., 2017), aging (Krukowski et al., 2020), diabetes (Abdulkarim et al., 2015; Harding et al., 2001), and cancer (Nguyen et al., 2018; Koromilas et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The ISR has been linked to diabetes.
source: Specifically, the ISR has been linked to neurodegenerative diseases (Ma et al., 2013), brain-injury induced dementia (Chou et al., 2017; Sen et al., 2017), aging (Krukowski et al., 2020), diabetes (Abdulkarim et al., 2015; Harding et al., 2001), and cancer (Nguyen et al., 2018; Koromilas et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The ISR has been linked to cancer.
source: Specifically, the ISR has been linked to neurodegenerative diseases (Ma et al., 2013), brain-injury induced dementia (Chou et al., 2017; Sen et al., 2017), aging (Krukowski et al., 2020), diabetes (Abdulkarim et al., 2015; Harding et al., 2001), and cancer (Nguyen et al., 2018; Koromilas et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The ternary complex consists of eIF2, Met-tRNAi, and GTP.
source: The TC consists of eIF2 (heterotrimer composed of an α, β, and γ subunit, containing a GTPase domain in its γ subunit), the initiator tRNA loaded with methionine (Met-tRNAi), and GTP (Algire et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: eIF2 is a heterotrimer composed of α, β, and γ subunits.
source: The TC consists of eIF2 (heterotrimer composed of an α, β, and γ subunit, containing a GTPase domain in its γ subunit), the initiator tRNA loaded with methionine (Met-tRNAi), and GTP (Algire et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: eIF2 requires GDP-to-GTP exchange for every round of cap-dependent translation initiation.
source: Crucially, for every round of cap-dependent translation initiation, eIF2 requires GDP-to-GTP exchange, catalyzed by its dedicated guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF), eIF2B.
evidence: This is established knowledge about translation initiation.

claim: eIF2B is the dedicated guanine nucleotide exchange factor for eIF2.
source: Crucially, for every round of cap-dependent translation initiation, eIF2 requires GDP-to-GTP exchange, catalyzed by its dedicated guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF), eIF2B.
evidence: This is established knowledge about eIF2B function.

claim: Many eIF2B mutations result in Vanishing White Matter Disease (VWMD).
source: Given its central role in controlling TC levels and mRNA translation, many eIF2B mutations result in an aberrant ISR and severe disease, such as Vanishing White Matter Disease (VWMD) (Leegwater et al., 2001; van der Knaap et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: eIF2B is a heterodecameric complex composed of two copies each of α, β, γ, δ, and ε subunits.
source: Molecularly, eIF2B is a large, heterodecameric complex composed of two copies each of an α, β, γ, δ, and ε subunit (Kashiwagi et al., 2016; Tsai et al., 2018; Zyryanova et al., 2018; Wortham et al., 2014; Gordiyenko et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Phosphorylation of eIF2 converts eIF2 from an eIF2B substrate to an eIF2B inhibitor.
source: It has long been established that phosphorylation of eIF2 (eIF2-P) converts eIF2 from an eIF2B substrate to an eIF2B inhibitor, leading to a reduction in GEF activity and ISR activation (Siekierka et al., 1982; Matts et al., 1983; Konieczny and Safer, 1983; Salimans et al., 1984; Rowlands et al., 1988).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Binding of eIF2-P to eIF2B allosterically switches eIF2B from its active A-State to an inhibited I-State.
source: However, we and others recently discovered that binding of the inhibitor eIF2-P to a distinct binding site — located on the face of the eIF2B complex opposite of the substrate-binding site — allosterically switches eIF2B from its active 'A-State' (which can readily engage eIF2 and catalyze nucleotide exchange) to an inhibited 'I-State' (Schoof et al., 2021a; Zyryanova et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to recent work by the authors and others.

claim: The decameric eIF2B holoenzyme is built from two eIF2Bβγδε tetramers and one eIF2Bα2 dimer.
source: The decameric holoenzyme is built from two eIF2Bβγδε tetramers and one eIF2Bα2 dimer (Tsai et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The eIF2Bε subunit harbors the enzyme's catalytic center.
source: The eIF2Bε subunit harbors the enzyme's catalytic center but only contains a small part of the binding surface of eIF2.
evidence: This is established knowledge about eIF2B structure and function.

claim: The specific enzyme activity of eIF2Bε in the eIF2Bβγδε tetramer is ~100 fold lower compared to the fully assembled eIF2B decamer.
source: Yet, even when embedded in the eIF2Bβγδε tetramer subcomplex, the specific enzyme activity (kcat/KM) of eIF2Bε is ~100 fold lower compared to the fully assembled eIF2B(αβγδε)2 decamer (tetramer kcat/KM = 0.07 min–1µM–1, decamer kcat/KM = 7.24 min–1µM–1), in which the substrate-interacting surface is further extended by bridging the twofold symmetric interface formed between the two tetrameric subcomplexes (a fourth interface, IF4 in eIF2Bδ') (Schoof et al., 2021a; Kenner et al., 2019; Kashiwagi et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work including the authors' previous study.

claim: ISRIB binds in a deep groove spanning across the symmetry interface of the two eIF2B tetramers.
source: This small molecule binds in a deep groove spanning across the symmetry interface of the two eIF2B tetramers and enhances its GEF activity (Sekine et al., 2015; Sidrauski et al., 2013; Sidrauski et al., 2015; Tsai et al., 2018; Zyryanova et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: ISRIB enhances eIF2B GEF activity.
source: This small molecule binds in a deep groove spanning across the symmetry interface of the two eIF2B tetramers and enhances its GEF activity (Sekine et al., 2015; Sidrauski et al., 2013; Sidrauski et al., 2015; Tsai et al., 2018; Zyryanova et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: ISRIB binding stabilizes eIF2B in the active A-State.
source: When eIF2Bα2 levels are saturating and eIF2B decamers are therefore fully assembled, ISRIB binding stabilizes eIF2B in the active 'A-State', reducing its affinity for the inhibitor eIF2-P (Schoof et al., 2021a; Zyryanova et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to recent work.

claim: The βH160D mutation blocked ISRIB-driven assembly of eIF2B tetramers into octamers in vitro.
source: We formerly observed that this missense mutation blocked ISRIB-driven assembly of eIF2B tetramers into octamers in vitro, underlining the importance of the H160 residue in stabilizing the octamer (Tsai et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: WT eIF2B tetramers readily assembled into octamers in the presence of ISRIB.
source: Consistent with our previous observations (Tsai et al., 2018), WT eIF2B tetramers readily assembled into octamers in the presence of ISRIB, whereas βH160D tetramers did not (Figure 1A, B).
evidence: Supported by analytical ultracentrifugation data shown in Figure 1A and citation to prior work.

claim: βH160D tetramers did not assemble into octamers in the presence of ISRIB.
source: Consistent with our previous observations (Tsai et al., 2018), WT eIF2B tetramers readily assembled into octamers in the presence of ISRIB, whereas βH160D tetramers did not (Figure 1A, B).
evidence: Supported by analytical ultracentrifugation data shown in Figure 1B and citation to prior work.

claim: Assembly of βH160D tetramers into the fully decameric holoenzyme by addition of the eIF2Bα2 dimer was not compromised.
source: In contrast, we found that assembly into the fully decameric holoenzyme by addition of the eIF2Bα2 dimer was not compromised (Figure 1C, D).
evidence: Supported by analytical ultracentrifugation data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: Titration of ISRIB assembled WT eIF2Bβδγε-F tetramers into octamers with EC50 = 170 ± 25 nM.
source: A titration of ISRIB readily assembled WT eIF2Bβδγε-F tetramers into octamers (EC50 = 170 ± 25 nM) but did not promote βH160D eIF2Bβδγε-F assembly into octamers, even at the highest concentrations tested (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by FRET assay data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: ISRIB did not promote βH160D eIF2Bβδγε-F assembly into octamers, even at the highest concentrations tested.
source: A titration of ISRIB readily assembled WT eIF2Bβδγε-F tetramers into octamers (EC50 = 170 ± 25 nM) but did not promote βH160D eIF2Bβδγε-F assembly into octamers, even at the highest concentrations tested (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by FRET assay data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Titration of eIF2Bα2 assembled WT eIF2Bβδγε-F tetramers into decamers with EC50 = 29 ± 3 nM.
source: By contrast and in agreement with the analytical ultracentrifugation data in Figure 1A–D, titration of eIF2Bα2 assembled both WT (EC50 = 29 ± 3 nM) and βH160D (EC50 = 33 ± 3 nM) eIF2Bβδγε-F tetramers into decamers with comparable efficiency (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by FRET assay data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Titration of eIF2Bα2 assembled βH160D eIF2Bβδγε-F tetramers into decamers with EC50 = 33 ± 3 nM.
source: By contrast and in agreement with the analytical ultracentrifugation data in Figure 1A–D, titration of eIF2Bα2 assembled both WT (EC50 = 29 ± 3 nM) and βH160D (EC50 = 33 ± 3 nM) eIF2Bβδγε-F tetramers into decamers with comparable efficiency (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by FRET assay data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: In the inhibited decameric conformation (I-State) induced by eIF2-P binding, ISRIB binding to eIF2B is impaired.
source: These properties are reminiscent of eIF2B's behavior in the presence of its inhibitor eIF2-P. In the inhibited decameric conformation (I-State) induced by eIF2-P binding, ISRIB binding to eIF2B is impaired (Schoof et al., 2021a; Zyryanova et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to recent work.

claim: WT and βH160D tetramers exhibited comparably low enzymatic activity.
source: Both WT and βH160D tetramers exhibited comparably low enzymatic activity.
evidence: Supported by nucleotide exchange assay data.

claim: ISRIB robustly enhanced WT tetramer activity but had no impact on βH160D tetramer activity.
source: The activity was robustly enhanced in WT octamers assembled from tetramers with ISRIB but, as expected, ISRIB had no impact on βH160D tetramer activity (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by nucleotide exchange assay data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: βH160D decamers were less active than WT decamers (t1/2 = 23.6 ± 0.8 min vs. 9.3 ± 1.0 min).
source: Intriguingly, βH160D decamers were less active than WT decamers (t1/2 = 23.6 ± 0.8 min vs. 9.3 ± 1.0 min, respectively) (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by nucleotide exchange assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The Vmax was significantly diminished by ~three fold for βH160D decamers when compared to WT decamers (WT Vmax = 1.86 ± 0.13 pmol min–1; βH160D Vmax = 0.66 ± 0.03 pmol min–1, two-sided t-test p=0.0045).
source: The Vmax (and consequently also the kcat) was significantly diminished by ~three fold for βH160D decamers when compared to WT decamers (WT Vmax = 1.86 ± 0.13 pmol min–1; βH160D Vmax = 0.66 ± 0.03 pmol min–1, two-sided t-test p=0.0045) suggesting that the βH160D mutation limits the intrinsic enzymatic activity of eIF2B (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by Michaelis-Menten kinetic analysis shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: The βH160D mutation limits the intrinsic enzymatic activity of eIF2B.
source: The Vmax (and consequently also the kcat) was significantly diminished by ~three fold for βH160D decamers when compared to WT decamers (WT Vmax = 1.86 ± 0.13 pmol min–1; βH160D Vmax = 0.66 ± 0.03 pmol min–1, two-sided t-test p=0.0045) suggesting that the βH160D mutation limits the intrinsic enzymatic activity of eIF2B (Figure 2D).
evidence: Inferred from the reduced Vmax observed in kinetic experiments.

claim: No significant difference in measured KM was detected between WT and βH160D decamers (WT KM = 0.36 ± 0.06 μM, βH160D KM = 0.19 ± 0.04 μM, two-sided t-test p=0.07).
source: In contrast, we could not detect a significant difference in measured KM (WT KM = 0.36 ± 0.06 μM, βH160D KM = 0.19 ± 0.04 μM, two-sided t-test p=0.07).
evidence: Supported by Michaelis-Menten kinetic analysis.

claim: eIF2 association with WT and βH160D decamers was monophasic.
source: eIF2 association with WT and βH160D decamers was monophasic, but dissociation was notably biphasic irrespective of eIF2 concentration, with a fast phase and a slow phase (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: Supported by SPR data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: eIF2 dissociation from WT and βH160D decamers was notably biphasic with a fast phase and a slow phase.
source: eIF2 association with WT and βH160D decamers was monophasic, but dissociation was notably biphasic irrespective of eIF2 concentration, with a fast phase and a slow phase (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: Supported by SPR data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: eIF2 binding to WT vs. βH160D decamers differed in the percentage of fast phase dissociation events (WT = 29%; βH160D = 67%).
source: Although the rate constants ka, kd fast, and kd slow were broadly comparable, eIF2 binding to WT vs. βH160D decamers differed in the percentage of fast phase dissociation events (WT = 29%; βH160D = 67%) (Figure 3A, B, Table 1).
evidence: Supported by SPR data shown in Figure 3A, B and Table 1.

claim: A larger fraction of substrate molecules dissociates rapidly from βH160D compared to WT decamers.
source: Thus, a larger fraction of substrate molecules dissociates rapidly from βH160D compared to WT decamers.
evidence: Inferred from the SPR data showing different percentages of fast phase dissociation.

claim: eIF2 dissociation from tetrameric eIF2B can be modeled using one phase association and dissociation.
source: In contrast to eIF2's interaction with decameric eIF2B, binding to WT tetramers could be modeled using one phase association and dissociation.
evidence: Supported by SPR data analysis.

claim: eIF2 dissociation from tetrameric eIF2B can be thought of as being 100% fast phase.
source: Indeed, eIF2 dissociation from tetrameric eIF2B can be thought of as being 100% fast phase as the dissociation constant was indistinguishable from the fast phase dissociation constant for both WT and βH160D (kd = 0.12 s–1) (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by SPR data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The fraction of eIF2 molecules that dissociate from decamers with fast phase kinetics may only be engaging eIF2B through interfaces 1–3.
source: The fraction of eIF2 molecules that dissociate from decamers with fast phase kinetics may therefore only be engaging eIF2B through interfaces 1–3 (interfaces 1 and 2 in eIF2Bε and interface 3 in eIF2Bβ).
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of dissociation kinetics between tetramers and decamers.

claim: The eIF2 molecules that dissociate with slow phase kinetics may additionally contact interface 4 in eIF2Bδ'.
source: In contrast, the eIF2 molecules that dissociate with slow phase kinetics may additionally contact interface 4 in eIF2Bδ', reaching across the central symmetry interface (Schoof et al., 2021a).
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of dissociation kinetics and supported by citation to prior work.

claim: At equilibrium the fast phase dissociation plays a small part in the engagement between eIF2 and WT eIF2B but plays a significant part in substrate engagement with βH160D decamers.
source: These data argue that at equilibrium the fast phase dissociation plays a small part in the engagement between eIF2 and WT eIF2B but plays a significant part in substrate engagement with βH160D decamers.
evidence: Inferred from the variable association time SPR experiments.

claim: The overall affinity of eIF2-P for WT and βH160D decamers was largely comparable (WT KD = 14 nM; βH160D KD = 8.1 nM).
source: The overall affinity of eIF2-P for both species was largely comparable (WT KD = 14 nM; βH160D KD = 8.1 nM) (Figure 3D, E).
evidence: Supported by SPR data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: No noticeable eIF2-P binding to WT tetramers was observed.
source: As expected owing to the absence of the dimeric eIF2Bα subunit, which constitutes part of the eIF2-P binding site, we observed no noticeable eIF2-P binding to WT tetramers (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by SPR data shown in Figure 3F and knowledge about the eIF2-P binding site.

claim: The βH160D decamer shares properties with the eIF2-P-bound decamer: reduced intrinsic GEF activity, impaired substrate binding, and insensitivity to ISRIB.
source: From these results, we conclude that the βH160D decamer shares a number of properties with the eIF2-P-bound decamer: (1) reduced intrinsic GEF activity, (2) impaired substrate binding, and (3) insensitivity to ISRIB.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented.

claim: The two tetramer halves of the βH160D decamer underwent a rocking motion that changed the angle between them by approximately 3.5°.
source: By superimposing the βH160D decamer structure and our previously published A-State structure (eIF2B-eIF2 complex, PDB ID: 6O81), we observed a significant difference in their overall architecture: the two tetramer halves of the βH160D decamer underwent a rocking motion that changed the angle between them by approximately 3.5° (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by cryo-EM structural analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The rocking motion in the βH160D decamer repositions the two tetramer halves in an orientation comparable to the I-State structure.
source: This rocking motion repositions the two tetramer halves in an orientation comparable to the I-State structure (eIF2B-eIF2αP complex, PDB ID: 6O9Z), although not reaching the 6° angle observed for the eIF2-P-inhibited decamer (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by cryo-EM structural comparison shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: In both the WT and the βH160D mutant, the two tetrameric halves can undergo rocking motions around the central axis.
source: We found the following: (1) in both the WT and the mutant, the two tetrameric halves can undergo rocking motions around the central axis; (2) the βH160D mutation shifts the mean conformation of the decamer towards the I-State; and (3) the βH160D dataset likely represents particles that follow a continuous conformation distribution, rather than a mixture of distinct A and I-State populations.
evidence: Supported by additional cryo-EM analysis described in Figure 4—figure supplements 3–5.

claim: The βH160D mutation shifts the mean conformation of the decamer towards the I-State.
source: We found the following: (1) in both the WT and the mutant, the two tetrameric halves can undergo rocking motions around the central axis; (2) the βH160D mutation shifts the mean conformation of the decamer towards the I-State; and (3) the βH160D dataset likely represents particles that follow a continuous conformation distribution, rather than a mixture of distinct A and I-State populations.
evidence: Supported by additional cryo-EM analysis described in Figure 4—figure supplements 3–5.

claim: The βH160D dataset likely represents particles that follow a continuous conformation distribution, rather than a mixture of distinct A and I-State populations.
source: We found the following: (1) in both the WT and the mutant, the two tetrameric halves can undergo rocking motions around the central axis; (2) the βH160D mutation shifts the mean conformation of the decamer towards the I-State; and (3) the βH160D dataset likely represents particles that follow a continuous conformation distribution, rather than a mixture of distinct A and I-State populations.
evidence: Supported by additional cryo-EM analysis described in Figure 4—figure supplements 3–5.

claim: The ISRIB binding pocket in the βH160D decamer was 3.3 Å wider in its long dimension than that of the A-State.
source: Comparing the βH160D decamer to A-State (eIF2-bound eIF2B) and I-State (eIF2α-P-bound eIF2B) structures, we noticed that its ISRIB binding pocket was 3.3 Å wider in its long dimension than that of the A-State (Figure 5A), again reminiscent of the I-State (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 5A and C.

claim: The widening of the ISRIB binding pocket can explain why ISRIB fails to assemble βH160D tetramers into octamers or affect GEF activity.
source: The widening of the binding pocket can explain why ISRIB fails to assemble βH160D tetramers into octamers or affect GEF activity.
evidence: Inferred from the structural observation of the widened ISRIB binding pocket.

claim: In the WT decamer, βH160 forms a π–π stacking interaction with δ'F452, which is lost in the βH160D eIF2B decamer.
source: In the WT decamer, βH160 forms a π–π stacking interaction with δ'F452, which is lost in the βH160D eIF2B decamer and leads to the retraction of the short loop bearing this residue (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The substrate eIF2α binding pocket was widened by 2.9 Å in the βH160D decamer structure compared to the eIF2B-eIF2 complex structure.
source: An overlay of the βH160D decamer structure with the eIF2B-eIF2 complex structure revealed that the substrate eIF2α binding pocket was widened by 2.9 Å (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The pocket widening is predicted to prevent eIF2 from properly engaging the fourth binding site on eIF2Bδ'.
source: This widening is predicted to prevent eIF2 from properly engaging the fourth binding site on eIF2Bδ' and hence turns the decameric eIF2B into conjoined tetramers such that only three of the four eIF2-eIF2B binding interfaces remain readily accessible to eIF2 binding.
evidence: Inferred from the structural observation of the widened eIF2α binding pocket.

claim: The inhibitor (eIF2α-P) binding site was not changed significantly in the βH160D decamer compared to the eIF2B-eIF2α-P complex structure.
source: By contrast, the inhibitor (eIF2α-P) binding site (Figure 5G) was not changed significantly compared to the eIF2B-eIF2α-P complex structure.
evidence: Supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The unchanged eIF2-P binding site is consistent with the similar binding affinities measured for eIF2-P towards the βH160D decamer and the WT decamer.
source: This observation is consistent with the similar binding affinities measured for eIF2-P towards the βH160D decamer and the WT decamer.
evidence: Inferred from the structural observation and SPR data.

claim: Both βH160D cell lines showed eIF2Bβ and eIF2Bε protein levels comparable to the unedited parental cells.
source: Critically, both βH160D cell lines showed eIF2Bβ and eIF2Bε protein levels comparable to the unedited parental cells, demonstrating that the mutation does not destabilize eIF2Bβ or other complex members and that compensatory mechanisms must normalize the gene dosage imbalance in clone #2 (Figure 6A; Wortham et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6A and citation to prior work.

claim: Constitutive, low-level activation of the ISR was observed in both βH160D clones, exemplified by elevated levels of ATF4 protein in the absence of stress.
source: We observed constitutive, low-level activation of the ISR in both clones, exemplified by elevated levels of ATF4 protein in the absence of stress (Figure 6A, lanes 5 and 9 vs lane 1).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: ATF4 induction was still responsive to induced stress with thapsigargin in βH160D lines.
source: ATF4 induction was still responsive to induced stress with thapsigargin (lanes 7 and 11) but could not be alleviated by ISRIB treatment in the βH160D lines, both in the absence or presence of stressor (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: ATF4 induction could not be alleviated by ISRIB treatment in the βH160D lines.
source: ATF4 induction was still responsive to induced stress with thapsigargin (lanes 7 and 11) but could not be alleviated by ISRIB treatment in the βH160D lines, both in the absence or presence of stressor (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: ATF4 mRNA levels remained unchanged between WT and the two βH160D clones.
source: ATF4 is translationally upregulated during the ISR and, accordingly, ATF4 mRNA levels remained unchanged between WT and the two βH160D clones (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Key ATF4 transcriptional targets (such as DDIT3, ASNS, and CARS) were upregulated in βH160D cells.
source: However, as expected, key ATF4 transcriptional targets (such as DDIT3, ASNS, and CARS) were upregulated in βH160D cells, confirming that increased ATF4 mRNA translation leads to production of active ATF4, which in turn activates transcription of its downstream stress-responsive genes (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Both βH160D cell lines displayed significantly reduced levels of basal protein synthesis (βH160D #1 cells: 47 ± 9.0%; βH160D #2 cells: 69 ± 7.3%, both compared to WT).
source: Both βH160D cell lines displayed significantly reduced levels of basal protein synthesis (βH160D #1 cells: 47 ± 9.0%; βH160D #2 cells: 69 ± 7.3%, both compared to WT), again consistent with constitutive activation of the ISR (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by puromycin incorporation assay data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: WT and βH160D cells did not differ in eIF2α phosphorylation levels.
source: WT and βH160D cells did not differ in eIF2α phosphorylation levels, underlining the observation that the impairment of eIF2B GEF activity caused by this mutation is sufficient to induce a constitutive ISR (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 3A-B).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A-B.

claim: Cell doubling time increased from 25.7 ± 3.6 h for WT cells to 38.4 ± 3.5 h for βH160D (#1) cells.
source: Phenotypically, the constitutive ISR activation was accompanied by slow cell growth: cell doubling time increased from 25.7 ± 3.6 h for WT cells to 38.4 ± 3.5 h for βH160D (#1) cells and could not be rescued by ISRIB treatment (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: Supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The slow growth of βH160D cells could not be rescued by ISRIB treatment.
source: Phenotypically, the constitutive ISR activation was accompanied by slow cell growth: cell doubling time increased from 25.7 ± 3.6 h for WT cells to 38.4 ± 3.5 h for βH160D (#1) cells and could not be rescued by ISRIB treatment (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: Supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3C.

claim: A single engineered H to D mutation in eIF2Bβ alters the conformation of the eIF2B decamer.
source: Here, we show that a single engineered H to D mutation in eIF2Bβ alters the conformation of the eIF2B decamer, resulting in altered dissociation kinetics of substrate eIF2, a ~ three fold reduction of intrinsic enzymatic activity, and resistance to ISRIB rescue.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings supported by the data presented.

claim: The βH160D mutation results in altered dissociation kinetics of substrate eIF2.
source: Here, we show that a single engineered H to D mutation in eIF2Bβ alters the conformation of the eIF2B decamer, resulting in altered dissociation kinetics of substrate eIF2, a ~ three fold reduction of intrinsic enzymatic activity, and resistance to ISRIB rescue.
evidence: Supported by SPR data showing biphasic dissociation kinetics.

claim: The βH160D mutation results in a ~three fold reduction of intrinsic enzymatic activity.
source: Here, we show that a single engineered H to D mutation in eIF2Bβ alters the conformation of the eIF2B decamer, resulting in altered dissociation kinetics of substrate eIF2, a ~ three fold reduction of intrinsic enzymatic activity, and resistance to ISRIB rescue.
evidence: Supported by Michaelis-Menten kinetic analysis.

claim: The βH160D mutation results in resistance to ISRIB rescue.
source: Here, we show that a single engineered H to D mutation in eIF2Bβ alters the conformation of the eIF2B decamer, resulting in altered dissociation kinetics of substrate eIF2, a ~ three fold reduction of intrinsic enzymatic activity, and resistance to ISRIB rescue.
evidence: Supported by FRET assays and cellular data showing no response to ISRIB.

claim: In cells, the βH160D hypomorphic mutation culminates in a constitutively activated low-level ISR.
source: In cells, this hypomorphic mutation culminates in a constitutively activated low-level ISR.
evidence: Supported by cellular data showing elevated ATF4, reduced protein synthesis, and slow growth.

claim: The conformational changes brought about by eIF2-P binding result in a specific enzymatic activity that is approximately 2 orders of magnitude reduced from that of the A-State.
source: The conformational changes brought about by eIF2-P binding result in a specific enzymatic activity (quantified in the specificity constant kcat/KM) that is approximately 2 orders of magnitude reduced from that of the A-State (Schoof et al., 2021a).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The βH160D mutation causes the specificity constant to drop by only ~2 fold.
source: By comparison, the βH160D mutation causes the specificity constant to drop by only ~2 fold (Figure 2).
evidence: Inferred from the kinetic data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Despite the comparatively small change in eIF2B activity, the βH160D mutation induces constitutive ISR activation.
source: Nevertheless, despite the comparatively small change in eIF2B activity, the mutation induces constitutive ISR activation, suggesting that cells are sensitive to small fluctuations in eIF2B GEF activity.
evidence: Inferred from the cellular data showing ISR activation despite modest enzymatic changes.

claim: Cells are sensitive to small fluctuations in eIF2B GEF activity.
source: Nevertheless, despite the comparatively small change in eIF2B activity, the mutation induces constitutive ISR activation, suggesting that cells are sensitive to small fluctuations in eIF2B GEF activity.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that a small change in activity leads to ISR activation.

claim: The βH160 residue is highly conserved amongst eukaryotes.
source: The βH160 residue is highly conserved amongst eukaryotes.
evidence: This is a statement about sequence conservation that can be verified through sequence databases.

claim: No variation has been reported at the βH160 position in the human genome.
source: To date, no variation has been reported at this position in the human genome.
evidence: This is a statement about the absence of reported variants in databases.

claim: Certain VWMD mutations may compromise eIF2B function through alteration of conformational state.
source: However, the mechanism by which the βH160D mutation impacts eIF2B activity raises the possibility that certain VWMD mutations may likewise compromise eIF2B function through alteration of conformational state.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings of the current study.

claim: The disease-associated βE213G mutation does not affect complex association but substantially reduces GEF activity.
source: The disease-associated βE213G mutation (ClinVar VCV000004336), for example, localized near the ISRIB pocket and far away from the catalytic center, reportedly does not affect complex association but substantially reduces GEF activity (Li et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: ISRIB is unable to rescue the βH160D defect.
source: Although ISRIB is unable to rescue the βH160D defect, it is plausible that other analogs (or molecules acting at a different site) with higher affinities than ISRIB may be able to overcome the charge repulsion and restore the A-State conformation, demonstrating the importance of continued endeavors to uncover molecules and strategies to inhibit or activate the ISR orthogonally.
evidence: Supported by the experimental data showing no ISRIB rescue.

claim: Other analogs with higher affinities than ISRIB may be able to overcome the charge repulsion and restore the A-State conformation in βH160D mutants.
source: Although ISRIB is unable to rescue the βH160D defect, it is plausible that other analogs (or molecules acting at a different site) with higher affinities than ISRIB may be able to overcome the charge repulsion and restore the A-State conformation, demonstrating the importance of continued endeavors to uncover molecules and strategies to inhibit or activate the ISR orthogonally.
evidence: This is speculation about potential therapeutic strategies.
